claim: Influential theories emphasize the importance of predictions in learning: we learn from feedback to the extent that it is surprising, and thus conveys new information.
source: Influential theories emphasize the importance of predictions in learning: we learn from feedback to the extent that it is surprising, and thus conveys new information.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established theories in the field.

claim: People leverage insights from response-based performance monitoring – outcome predictions and confidence – to control learning from feedback.
source: Specifically, we propose that people leverage insights from response-based performance monitoring – outcome predictions and confidence – to control learning from feedback.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, tested through modeling and empirical data.

claim: People who are better at calibrating their confidence to the precision of their outcome predictions learn more quickly.
source: In line with predictions from a Bayesian inference model, we find that people who are better at calibrating their confidence to the precision of their outcome predictions learn more quickly.
evidence: This finding is supported by both computational modeling predictions and empirical behavioral data.

claim: EEG signatures of feedback processing are sensitive to the accuracy of, and confidence in, post-response outcome predictions.
source: Further in line with our proposal, EEG signatures of feedback processing are sensitive to the accuracy of, and confidence in, post-response outcome predictions.
evidence: This is supported by EEG data showing modulation of feedback-related ERP components.

claim: Online predictions and confidence serve to calibrate neural error signals to improve the efficiency of learning.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that online predictions and confidence serve to calibrate neural error signals to improve the efficiency of learning.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined behavioral and neural findings.

claim: Feedback drives learning to the degree that it is unexpected and provides new information in the form of prediction errors.
source: Across domains it is thought that feedback drives learning to the degree that it is unexpected and, hence, provides new information, for example in the form of prediction errors that express the discrepancy between actual and expected outcomes (McGuire et al., 2014; Yu and Dayan, 2005; Behrens et al., 2007; Diederen and Schultz, 2015; Diederen et al., 2016; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Faisal et al., 2008; Sutton and Barto, 1998; Wolpert et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The same feedback can be caused by multiple sources: errors in knowledge about what to do or errors in execution.
source: Yet, the same feedback can be caused by multiple sources: we may be wrong about what is the correct thing to do, or we may know what to do but accidentally still do the wrong thing (McDougle et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and logical reasoning about sources of error.

claim: When people know they made an execution error, they should discount learning about action-outcome mappings.
source: When we know we did the latter, we should discount learning about the former (McDougle et al., 2019; Parvin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Performance monitoring could reduce surprise about feedback and uncertainty about its causes by providing information about execution errors.
source: Performance monitoring, that is the internal evaluation of one's own actions, could reduce surprise about feedback and uncertainty about its causes by providing information about execution errors.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on logical inference about the role of performance monitoring.

claim: People are often robustly aware of their response errors in simple categorical choices.
source: In simple categorical choices, people are often robustly aware of their response errors (Maier et al., 2011; Yeung et al., 2004; Riesel et al., 2013; Maier et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Awareness of response errors is reflected in neural markers of error detection.
source: and this awareness is reflected in neural markers of error detection (Murphy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study showing neural correlates.

claim: Both error detection and feedback processing are sensitive to error magnitude.
source: Although errors are often studied in simple categorization tasks in which responses are either correct or incorrect, in many tasks, errors occur on a graded scale (e.g. a dart can miss the target narrowly or by a large margin), and both error detection, as well as feedback processing are sensitive to error magnitude (Luft et al., 2014; Ulrich and Hewig, 2014; Frömer et al., 2016a; Arbel and Donchin, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: People are able to report gradual errors reasonably accurately.
source: People are even able to report gradual errors reasonably accurately (Kononowicz et al., 2019; Akdoğan and Balcı, 2017; Kononowicz and van Wassenhove, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: People rely on internal models to predict the outcome of movements based on an efference copy of a motor command.
source: This ability may be afforded by reliance on internal models to predict the outcome of movements (Wolpert and Flanagan, 2001), for example, based on an efference copy of a motor command.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established theory.

claim: If outcome predictions perfectly matched execution errors, the remaining mismatch between predicted and obtained feedback could serve as a reliable basis for adaptation.
source: In fact, if these predictions perfectly matched the execution error that occurred, the remaining mismatch between predicted and obtained feedback (sensory prediction error) could serve as a reliable basis for adaptation and render feedback maximally informative about the mapping from actions to outcomes (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on inference and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Error detection is far less certain than in the ideal scenario, and the true cause of feedback often remains uncertain.
source: Although participants are able to evaluate their own performance reasonably well, error detection is far less certain than outlined in the ideal scenario above, and the true cause of feedback often remains uncertain to some extent.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of human performance monitoring.

claim: People are critically sensitive to uncertainty and learn more from feedback when they expect it to be more informative.
source: People are critically sensitive to uncertainty, and learn more from feedback when they expect it to be more informative (McGuire et al., 2014; Schiffer et al., 2017; Bland and Schaefer, 2012; Nassar et al., 2010; O'Reilly, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Uncertainty about what caused a given feedback inevitably renders it less informative and should be taken into account when learning from it.
source: Uncertainty about what caused a given feedback inevitably renders it less informative, similar to decreases in reliability, and this uncertainty should be taken into account when learning from it.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the impact of uncertainty on learning.

claim: Confidence could support adaptive learning from feedback by providing a read-out of the subjective precision of predicted outcomes.
source: Confidence could support such adaptive learning from feedback by providing a read-out of the subjective precision of predicted outcomes (Nassar et al., 2010; Vaghi et al., 2017; Meyniel et al., 2015; Pouget et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Confidence may rely on shared neural correlates with error detection.
source: possibly relying on shared neural correlates of confidence with error detection (Boldt and Yeung, 2015; van den Berg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing neural overlap.

claim: People could leverage confidence to calibrate their use of online predictions, similar to its role in regulating learning of transition probabilities.
source: Similar to its role in regulating learning of transition probabilities (Meyniel et al., 2015; Meyniel and Dehaene, 2017), information seeking/exploration in decision making (Desender et al., 2018a; Boldt et al., 2019), and hierarchical reasoning (Sarafyazd and Jazayeri, 2019), people could leverage confidence to calibrate their use of online predictions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to related work and inference about the role of confidence.

claim: People learn more about advice givers when they are more confident in the choices that advice is about.
source: In line with this suggestion, people learn more about advice givers when they are more confident in the choices that advice is about (Carlebach and Yeung, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: The more confident you are about the exact landing position, the more surprised you should be when you find that landing position to be different.
source: In the throwing example above, the more confident you are about the exact landing position of the dart, the more surprised you should be when you find that landing position to be different
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between confidence and surprise.

claim: You should learn more when you are more confident, assuming that your predictions are in fact more precise when you are more confident.
source: Thus, you should learn more when you are more confident. However, this reasoning assumes that your predictions are in fact more precise when you are more confident, i.e., that your confidence is well calibrated (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a logical inference illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Performance monitoring – error detection and confidence – adaptively regulates learning from feedback.
source: In the present study, we tested the hypothesis that performance monitoring – error detection and confidence (Yeung and Summerfield, 2012) – adaptively regulates learning from feedback.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Error detection and confidence afford better learning, with confidence mediating the relationship between outcome predictions and feedback.
source: This hypothesis predicts that error detection and confidence afford better learning, with confidence mediating the relationship between outcome predictions and feedback, and that learning is compromised when confidence is mis-calibrated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the hypothesis and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Learning is compromised when confidence is mis-calibrated.
source: This hypothesis predicts that error detection and confidence afford better learning, with confidence mediating the relationship between outcome predictions and feedback, and that learning is compromised when confidence is mis-calibrated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the hypothesis and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Neural correlates of feedback processing (FRN and P3a) should integrate information about post-response outcome predictions and confidence.
source: It further predicts that established neural correlates of feedback processing, such as the feedback-related negativity (FRN) and the P3a (Ullsperger et al., 2014a), should integrate information about post-response outcome predictions and confidence.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the hypothesis about neural mechanisms.

claim: An error that could be predicted based on internal knowledge of how an action was executed should not yield a large surprise (P3a) or reward prediction error (FRN) signal.
source: That is to say, an error that could be predicted based on internal knowledge of how an action was executed should not yield a large surprise (P3a) or reward prediction error (FRN) signal in response to an external indicator of the error (feedback).
evidence: This is a prediction about neural responses based on the hypothesis.

claim: Any prediction error should be more surprising when predictions were made with higher confidence.
source: However, any prediction error should be more surprising when predictions were made with higher confidence.
evidence: This is a prediction about the modulation of surprise by confidence.

claim: The precision of outcome predictions (correlation between predicted and actual outcomes) should increase with confidence.
source: (1) The precision of outcome predictions (i.e. the correlation between predicted and actual outcomes) should increase with confidence.
evidence: This is a key behavioral prediction of the hypothesis.

claim: Learners with superior calibration of confidence to the precision of their outcome predictions should learn more quickly.
source: (2) Learners with superior calibration of confidence to the precision of their outcome predictions should learn more quickly.
evidence: This is a key behavioral prediction of the hypothesis.

claim: The optimally calibrated Bayesian learner with performance monitoring outperforms both a feedback-only learner and a learner with outcome prediction but no confidence calibration.
source: We find that performance improves as the amount of insight into the agent's performance increases (Figure 1F): The optimally calibrated Bayesian learner with performance monitoring outperforms both other models.
evidence: This finding is demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In the Bayesian learner with performance monitoring model, confidence varies with the precision of predictions.
source: Further, in line with our behavioral predictions, we find in this model that confidence varies with the precision of predictions (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is shown through model simulations illustrated in Figure 2A and supplement.

claim: In the Bayesian learner with performance monitoring model, agents with superior Confidence Calibration learn better.
source: and, when varying the fidelity of confidence as a read-out of precision (Confidence Calibration), agents with superior Confidence Calibration learn better (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through model simulations illustrated in Figure 2B and supplement.

claim: Predicted outcomes and actual outcomes were positively correlated in participants' behavior.
source: As expected, predicted outcomes and actual outcomes were positively correlated, indicating that participants could broadly indicate the direction and magnitude of their errors.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The relationship between predicted and actual outcomes was stronger for predictions made with higher confidence.
source: Crucially, this relationship between predicted and actual outcomes was stronger for predictions made with higher confidence (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: Both outcome predictions and confidence calibration improved across blocks, suggestive of learning at the level of performance monitoring.
source: In addition to this expected pattern, we found that both outcome predictions, as well as confidence calibration, improved across blocks, suggestive of learning at the level of performance monitoring (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Confidence increases as the discrepancy between predicted and actual outcome decreases.
source: Consistent with our assumption that Confidence tracks the precision of predictions, we find that it increases as the discrepancy between predicted and actual outcome decreases.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis in Table 2.

claim: Confidence was higher for larger errors, presumably because their direction is easier to judge.
source: Confidence was also higher for larger errors, presumably because their direction (i.e. overshoot or undershoot) is easier to judge.
evidence: This is an empirical finding with a speculative explanation.

claim: The relationships of confidence with both the precision of the prediction and error magnitude changed across blocks.
source: The relationships with both the precision of the prediction and error magnitude changed across blocks, and confidence increased across blocks as well.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis in Table 2.

claim: Participants with better confidence calibration showed greater performance improvements during the experiment.
source: Thus, participants with better confidence calibration showed greater performance improvements during the experiment.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis shown in Figure 2D and Table 3.

claim: Confidence Calibration did not significantly correlate with overall performance.
source: Importantly, Confidence Calibration did not significantly correlate with overall performance (Figure 2D inset), supporting the assumption that confidence calibration relates to learning (performance change), rather than performance per se.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Confidence calibration was not correlated with individual differences in response variance.
source: Confidence calibration was also not correlated with individual differences in response variance (r = - 2.07e-4, 95% CI = [−0.31, 0.31], p=0.999)
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: The interaction of confidence calibration and block was robust to controlling for running average response variance.
source: and the interaction of confidence calibration and block was robust to controlling for running average response variance (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a control analysis.

claim: Sensory prediction error (SPE) decreased as confidence increased.
source: Consistent with our assumption that confidence tracks the precision of predictions, SPE decreased as confidence increased (b = −71.20, p>0.001)
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis in Supplementary file 5.

claim: All error signals (Error Magnitude, RPE, SPE) decreased significantly across blocks.
source: All error signals further decreased significantly across blocks (Error Magnitude: b = - 37.10, p<0.001, RPE: b = 36.26, p<0.001, SPE: b = - 17.54, p<0.001, block wise comparisons significant only from block 1 to 2 Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Controlling for error magnitude eliminated block effects on SPE but the main effect of Confidence on SPE prevailed.
source: Controlling for error magnitude notably reduced linear block effects on RPE (b = 36.26 to b = 10.3). It further eliminated block effects on SPE: b = −17.54 to b = 3.65, p=0.274, as well as the interaction of confidence and Block (b = 0.10, p=0.984), while the hypothesized main effect of Confidence prevailed (b = −60.12, p<0.001).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a control analysis in Supplementary file 7.

claim: FRN amplitude decreased with more positive-going RPEs.
source: As predicted, FRN amplitude decreased with more positive-going RPEs (b = 1.43, p<0.001, Figure 4C)
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 4C and Table 4.

claim: Error magnitude and SPE did not significantly affect FRN amplitude.
source: In contrast, error magnitude and SPE did not significantly affect FRN amplitude
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis in Table 4.

claim: FRN amplitude reflects the degree to which feedback is better than predicted, with outcome predictions incorporating information about likely execution errors.
source: We conclude that FRN amplitude reflects the degree to which feedback is better than predicted, and critically, that the outcome predictions incorporate information about likely execution errors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FRN analysis results.

claim: P3a amplitude significantly increased with increasing SPEs.
source: As predicted, our analyses showed that P3a amplitude significantly increased with increasing SPEs, in line with the idea of stronger violations of expectations by less accurately predicted outcomes (Figure 4G and I, Table 5)
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 4G, I and Table 5.

claim: P3a amplitude increased with increasing Confidence.
source: and with increasing Confidence (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 4G, H and Table 5.

claim: P3a amplitude decreased across blocks, perhaps reflecting decreased motivational relevance of feedback as participants improved.
source: In addition, P3a amplitude decreased across blocks, perhaps reflecting decreased motivational relevance of feedback as participants improved their performance and predictions (Walentowska et al., 2016; Severo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an empirical finding with a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: P3b amplitude increased with increasing SPE.
source: P3b amplitude increased with increasing SPE (Figure 5B,E)
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 5B, E and Table 6.

claim: The SPE effect on P3b decreased across blocks.
source: As for P3a, this SPE effect decreased across blocks
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis in Table 6.

claim: Overall P3b amplitude decreased across blocks, suggesting that participants made less use of the feedback as they improved on the task.
source: and so did overall P3b amplitude, suggesting that participants made less use of the feedback as they improved on the task (Fischer and Ullsperger, 2013).
evidence: This is an empirical finding with an interpretation supported by citation.

claim: P3b amplitude increased with negative-going RPE (worse-than-expected outcomes).
source: P3b amplitude also increased with negative-going RPE (Figure 5B,C), hence, for worse-than-expected outcomes, replicating previous work (Ullsperger et al., 2014a; Fischer and Ullsperger, 2014).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 5B, C and Table 6.

claim: The RPE effect on P3b was significantly modulated by Confidence and Block.
source: This RPE effect was significantly modulated by Confidence and Block, indicating that the main effect needs to be interpreted with caution, and the relationship between P3b and RPE is more nuanced than previous literature suggested.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis in Table 6.

claim: In the first block, P3b amplitude was highest for large negative RPE and high Confidence, whereas in the last block it was highest for large negative RPE and low Confidence.
source: As shown in Figure 5D in the first block, P3b amplitude was highest for large negative RPE and high Confidence, whereas in the last block it was highest for large negative RPE and low Confidence (see below for follow-up analyses).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: P3b amplitude increased with decreasing Error Magnitude (better outcomes).
source: In line with previous findings (Pfabigan et al., 2014; Ernst and Steinhauser, 2018), we further observed significant increases of P3b amplitude with decreasing Error Magnitude, thus, with better outcomes (Figure 5B,F, Table 5).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis shown in Figure 5B, F and Table 6.

claim: Predicted Error Magnitude interacted with Confidence and Block in affecting P3b amplitude.
source: Confirming its relevance for the earlier interaction involving RPE, Predicted Error Magnitude indeed interacted with Confidence and Block.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the EEG data analysis in Table 7.

claim: In the first block, P3b significantly increased with higher Confidence and decreased significantly more with increasing Predicted Error Magnitude as Confidence increased.
source: Consistent with confidence-based regulation of learning, a follow-up analysis showed that in the first block, P3b significantly increased with higher Confidence, and importantly decreased significantly more with increasing Predicted Error Magnitude as Confidence increased (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a follow-up analysis in Supplementary file 8.

claim: P3b on trial n-1 mediated the relationship between error magnitude on trial n-1 and the improvement on the current trial in the first block.
source: A follow-up analysis confirmed that P3b mediated the relationship between previous error magnitude and improvement in the first block (b = 0.06, p<0.001, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a follow-up analysis in Supplementary file 10.

claim: Participants' behavior displayed hallmarks of error monitoring such that outcome predictions tracked factual errors in both direction and magnitude.
source: Participants' behavior displayed hallmarks of error monitoring (Kononowicz et al., 2019; Akdoğan and Balcı, 2017; Kononowicz and van Wassenhove, 2019), such that outcome predictions tracked factual errors in both direction and magnitude.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings supported by citations to related work.

claim: Confidence reflected the precision of participants' outcome predictions.
source: Crucially, extending those previous findings, our empirical results align with unique predictions based on our hypothesis: Confidence reflected the precision of participants' outcome predictions
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings.

claim: Participants with superior calibration of their confidence judgments to the accuracy of their predictions learned better than those with poorer calibration.
source: and participants with superior calibration of their confidence judgments to the accuracy of their predictions learned better than those with poorer calibration.
evidence: This is a summary of behavioral findings.

claim: The empirical confidence calibration effect on learning is unlikely to be a consequence of better overall ability or the 'unskilled and unaware effect'.
source: Therefore, the empirical confidence calibration effect on learning is unlikely to be a consequence of better overall ability as described in the 'unskilled and unaware effect' (Kruger and Dunning, 1999) or of the dependence of confidence calibration (or metacognitive sensitivity) on performance (Fleming and Lau, 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings ruling out alternative explanations.

claim: The finding supports the hypothesis that confidence supports learning via optimized feedback processing.
source: Instead, the finding supports our hypothesis that confidence supports learning via optimized feedback processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral findings.

claim: The main impact of error monitoring is to reduce the surprise about outcomes.
source: The main impact of error monitoring is to reduce the surprise about outcomes.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the study's findings.

claim: A given outcome is less surprising the better it matches the predicted outcome.
source: All else being equal, a given outcome is less surprising the better it matches the predicted outcome.
evidence: This is a logical inference about surprise and prediction.

claim: Reducing surprise by taking response-based outcome predictions into account led to more accurate updating of internal representations and superior learning in computational models.
source: In our computational models, reducing surprise by taking response-based outcome predictions into account led to more accurate updating of internal representations supporting action selection and thus superior learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling.

claim: As deviations from the goal were predicted with higher confidence, these more precise outcome predictions enhanced the surprise elicited by a given prediction error.
source: Specifically, as deviations from the goal were predicted with higher confidence, these more precise outcome predictions enhanced the surprise elicited by a given prediction error.
evidence: This is a mechanism identified in the computational model.

claim: Agents and participants learned more from feedback when confidence in their predictions had been high.
source: Thus, a notable finding revealed by our simulations and empirical data is that, counterintuitively, agents and participants learned more from feedback when confidence in their predictions had been high.
evidence: This is a key finding from both modeling and empirical data.

claim: The results align with previous findings of larger P3a amplitude for metacognitive mismatch.
source: Our results align with previous findings of larger P3a amplitude for metacognitive mismatch (Butterfield and Mangels, 2003)
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous literature.

claim: The results offer a computational mechanism underlying the theory that feedback about errors committed with high confidence attracts more attention and leads to hypercorrection.
source: and offer a computational mechanism underlying previous theorizing that feedback about errors committed with high confidence attracts more attention, and therefore leads to hypercorrection (Butterfield and Metcalfe, 2006; Butterfield and Metcalfe, 2001).
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous theoretical work.

claim: The results shed new light on the claim that error monitoring and confidence are tightly intertwined.
source: By reconceptualizing error detection as outcome prediction, our results shed new light on the well-supported claim that error monitoring and confidence are tightly intertwined (Boldt and Yeung, 2015; Yeung and Summerfield, 2012; Charles and Yeung, 2019; Desender et al., 2018b; Desender et al., 2019)
evidence: This is a theoretical contribution connecting to previous literature.

claim: The results forge valuable links between research on performance monitoring and on learning under uncertainty.
source: and forge valuable links between research on performance monitoring (Ullsperger et al., 2014a; Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Ullsperger et al., 2014b) and on learning under uncertainty (McGuire et al., 2014; Behrens et al., 2007; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Nassar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical contribution connecting different research areas.

claim: The results provide further evidence to the growing literature on the role of confidence in learning and behavioral adaptation.
source: In doing so, our results provide further evidence to the growing literature on the role of confidence in learning and behavioral adaptation (Meyniel and Dehaene, 2017; Desender et al., 2018a; Boldt et al., 2019; Colizoli et al., 2018).
evidence: This connects the current findings to a broader literature.

claim: Unlike the Bayesian agents, participants exhibited signatures of learning not only at the level of first order performance, but also at the level of performance monitoring.
source: Unlike our Bayesian agents, participants exhibited signatures of learning not only at the level of first order performance, but also at the level of performance monitoring.
evidence: This is an observation about differences between model and human behavior.

claim: The precision of participants' outcome predictions increased as learning progressed.
source: The precision of their outcome predictions increased as learning progressed, as did confidence.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from the behavioral data.

claim: In motor learning, individuals prefer and learn better from feedback following successful trials compared to error trials.
source: Indeed, when practicing complex motor tasks, individuals prefer and learn better from feedback following successful trials compared to error trials (Chiviacowsky and Wulf, 2007; Chiviacowsky and Wulf, 2002; Chiviacowsky and Wulf, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The P3b component scales with the amount of information provided by a stimulus.
source: In our study, the P3b component, previously shown to scale with the amount of information provided by a stimulus (Cockburn and Holroyd, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The P3b component scales with the amount of learning from a stimulus.
source: and the amount of learning from a stimulus (Fischer and Ullsperger, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: P3b was sensitive to both RPE and SPE, indicating that multiple learning mechanisms may act in parallel.
source: was sensitive to both RPE and SPE, indicating that multiple learning mechanisms may act in parallel, supported by different aspects of feedback.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the P3b findings.

claim: Recent work in rodents shows that prediction error signals encode multiple features of outcomes.
source: Our findings resonate with recent work in rodents showing that prediction error signals encode multiple features of outcomes (Langdon et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal research.

claim: Prediction error signals are based on distributed representations of predictions.
source: and are based on distributed representations of predictions (Dabney et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.

claim: Encoding of multiple features of outcomes may help credit assignment and support learning at multiple levels.
source: This encoding of multiple features of outcomes, like the uncertainty in predictions, may help credit assignment and support learning at multiple levels.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the function of distributed representations.

claim: Feedback evaluation is fundamentally affected by an individual's internal representations of their own performance at the time of feedback.
source: Taken together, our findings provide evidence that feedback evaluation is fundamentally affected by an individual's internal representations of their own performance at the time of feedback.
evidence: This is a main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Internal representations of performance influence how people learn and which beliefs they will have and which actions they will take.
source: These internal representations in turn influence how people learn and thus which beliefs they will have and which actions they will take, driving what internal and external states they will encounter in the future.
evidence: This is a broader theoretical claim about the implications of the findings.

claim: The study is a first step toward elucidating the recursive process of performance optimization via internal performance monitoring and monitoring of external task outcomes.
source: The present study is a first step toward elucidating this recursive process of performance optimization via internal performance monitoring and monitoring of external task outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution and scope of the study.

claim: The experiment included 40 participants (13 males) with an average age of 25.8 years.
source: The experimental study included 40 participants (13 males) whose average age was 25.8 years (SD = 4.3)
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: The mean handedness score of participants was 63.96, indicating most participants were right-handed.
source: and whose mean handedness score (Oldfield, 1971) was 63.96 (SD = 52.09; i.e., most participants were right-handed).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Participants' primary goal in the task was to learn to produce an initially unknown time interval.
source: Participants were instructed that their primary goal in this task is to learn to produce an initially unknown time interval.
evidence: This describes the task instructions given to participants.

claim: The target interval in the time-estimation task was 1504 ms.
source: Participants' task was to terminate an initially unknown target interval of 1504 ms from tone onset, by pressing a response key with their left hand.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the experimental task.

claim: A supra-second duration was chosen to make the task sufficiently difficult.
source: We chose a supra-second duration to make the task sufficiently difficult (Luft et al., 2014).
evidence: This explains a design choice with citation support.

claim: The experiment comprised five blocks of 50 trials each.
source: The experiment comprised five blocks of 50 trials each, with self-paced rests between blocks.
evidence: This describes the structure of the experiment.

claim: EEG data were recorded from 64 Ag/AgCl electrodes.
source: Using BrainVision recorder software (Brain Products, München, Germany) we recorded EEG data from 64 Ag/AgCl electrodes mounted in an electrode cap (ECI Inc), referenced against Cz at a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording setup.

claim: The FRN was quantified as peak-to-peak amplitude at electrode FCz as the difference between the minimum voltage in a window from 200 to 300 ms post-feedback onset and the preceding positive maximum.
source: The FRN was quantified in single-trial ERP waveforms as peak-to-peak amplitude at electrode FCz, specifically as the difference between the minimum voltage in a window from 200 to 300 ms post-feedback onset and the preceding positive maximum in a window from −100 to 0 ms relative to the detected negative peak.
evidence: This describes the method for quantifying the FRN component.

claim: P3a was quantified as the average voltage within an interval from 330 to 430 ms after feedback onset across a fronto-central region of interest.
source: Accordingly, the P3a was quantified on single trials as the average voltage within an interval from 330 to 430 ms after feedback onset across all electrodes within a fronto-central region of interest (ROI: F1, Fz, F2, FC1, FCz, FC2, C1, Cz, C2).
evidence: This describes the method for quantifying the P3a component.

claim: P3b amplitude was quantified as the average voltage within a 416–516 ms interval post-feedback across a parietally-focused region of interest.
source: P3b amplitude was quantified in single trials as the average voltage within a 416–516 ms interval post-feedback across all electrodes within a parietally-focused region of interest (ROI: CP1, CPz, CP2, P1, Pz, P2, PO3, POz, PO4).
evidence: This describes the method for quantifying the P3b component.

claim: Sensory prediction error (SPE) was determined as the absolute difference between predicted and actual interval length.
source: SPE was determined as the absolute difference between predicted and actual interval length: |Prediction – Feedback|.
evidence: This describes how SPE was operationalized in the analysis.

claim: Reward prediction error (RPE) was computed as the difference between the absolute predicted error and the absolute actual error.
source: RPE was computed as the difference between the absolute predicted error and the absolute actual error as revealed by feedback: |Prediction| – |Feedback|.
evidence: This describes how RPE was operationalized in the analysis.

claim: Confidence calibration was quantified as each participant's correlation of confidence and SPE across all trials, controlling for average error magnitude per block.
source: We quantified confidence calibration as each participant's correlation of confidence and SPE (absolute deviation of the prediction from the actual outcome) across all trials, controlling for average error magnitude per block to account for shared changes in our confidence calibration measure with performance.
evidence: This describes how confidence calibration was operationalized in the analysis.
